title: Cellist 'emotional' at being able to play again after major crash injury

input.lead: Cellist Clara Simpson was left with long-term injuries in a crash on her way to work
input.summary: Cellist Clara Simpson was left with long-term injuries in a crash on her way to work
input.evidence_text: A musician who was seriously injured in a crash has said that being able to play her instrument again for just a few minutes felt like "getting part of herself back" Clara Simpson was traveling from Manchester to Sheffield for her first day in a teaching role at Sheffield Music Academy when the car in which she was a passenger hit a large patch of ice and flipped onto its roof The incident, on A57 Snake Pass on 1 March, 2025, left the then 26-year-old in hospital for ten days with two fractured vertebrae The 28-year-old said: "It was the most terrifying experience of my life. When I was told I'd broken my neck, I genuinely thought everything I'd worked so hard for was over." Originally from Toronto in Canada, Clara moved to Manchester in 2021 to complete her postgraduate studies, and has since worked as a freelance classical cellist, touring and performing internationally Following the crash, she developed a condition which weakened one of her vocal cords after surgery through the front of her neck to treat her spine

title: Medal of Cheadle Hulme hero killed in last week of WW1 auctioned

input.lead: James Kirk was shot while defending comrades in the final days of the conflict, auctioneers say
input.summary: James Kirk was shot while defending comrades in the final days of the conflict, auctioneers say
input.evidence_text: Medal of Cheadle Hulme hero killed in last week of WW1 auctioned - BBC News Image source, Noonans Image caption, Second lieutenant James Kirk was killed in the last week of World War One By Stewart Whittingham North West Published 27 September 2026 A Victoria Cross awarded to a soldier who was killed while defending comrades in the last week of World War One is being put up for auction. James Kirk, from Cheadle Hulme, Greater Manchester, died under heavy machine gun fire as he protected soldiers building a bridge in France in November 1918. The 21-year-old second lieutenant carried on fighting even after being shot in the face, having paddled across a canal to single-handedly confront German gunners. His medal is being sold by London auctioneers Noonans on 7 October and is expected to fetch between £100,000 and £160,000. Noonans said Kirk "paid the ultimate sacrifice" as he sought to defend the Royal Engineers who were were trying to bridge the Oise Canal during the Battle of Sambre on 4 November 1918. Kirk took a Lewis machine gun and four magazines and paddled himself across the waterway on a raft made from petrol tins and cork floats "under a most intense machine gun barrage", Noonans said. Image source, Noonans Image caption, James Kirk was awarded the Victoria Cross for his bravery The auctioneers added: "The bank bristled with machine guns. "He set up his Lewis gun at 10 yards range and fired off the whole of his ammunition. "Further ammunition was paddled across to him on the raft and he continued firing, covering the Royal Engineers in their task. "He was wounded in the arm and the face but still fired continuously from a most exposed position until he was shot through the head and fell dead over his gun." Image source, PA Media Image caption, Huge crowds gather

input.summary: The hero firefighter who died trying to save a life More than 25 years after Sub Officer Paul Metcalf died trying to rescue a teenager from Hawkshaw's Simons Lodge, an FBU Red Plaque at Ramsbottom Fire Station honours the hero whose sacrifice transfor News Neal Keeling Chief repo
input.evidence_text: The hero firefighter who died trying to save a life More than 25 years after Sub Officer Paul Metcalf died trying to rescue a teenager from Hawkshaw's Simons Lodge, an FBU Red Plaque at Ramsbottom Fire Station honours the hero whose sacrifice transfor News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 16:43, 27 Sep 2026 Updated 17:00, 27 Sep 2026 It was an act of heroism which ended in tragedy. But every firefighter in the UK owes a debt to Paul Metcalf who died trying in vain to save the life of a teenager On a balmy autumn Sunday in 1999 Sub Officer Metcalf, based at Ramsbottom Fire Station and a crew answered a call. A boy had vanished under the surface at Simons Lodge, Hawkshaw. He had slipped into the water from a rope swing hanging from a tree as he tested the temperature with Super fit Mr Metcalf, aged 40, and a karate black belt, dived in but his non-floating rope became snagged on an underwater branch. As colleagues and police pulled the line to bring him ashore, unaware it was caught, he was pulled under water Despite the valiant efforts of two colleagues to save him it took 15 minutes to recover him and he died soon after in hospital But the legacy of Paul's death was that it led directly to the introduction of water safety and rescue equipment on frontline fire appliances nationally and the replacement of traditional hemp lines with floating nylon line

input.evidence_text: The hero firefighter who died trying to save a life More than 25 years after Sub Officer Paul Metcalf died trying to rescue a teenager from Hawkshaw's Simons Lodge, an FBU Red Plaque at Ramsbottom Fire Station honours the hero whose sacrifice transfor News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 16:43, 27 Sep 2026 Updated 17:00, 27 Sep 2026 It was an act of heroism which ended in tragedy. But every firefighter in the UK owes a debt to Paul Metcalf who died trying in vain to save the life of a teenager On a balmy autumn Sunday in 1999 Sub Officer Metcalf, based at Ramsbottom Fire Station and a crew answered a call. A boy had vanished under the surface at Simons Lodge, Hawkshaw. He had slipped into the water from a rope swing hanging from a tree as he tested the temperature with Super fit Mr Metcalf, aged 40, and a karate black belt, dived in but his non-floating rope became snagged on an underwater branch. As colleagues and police pulled the line to bring him ashore, unaware it was caught, he was pulled under water Despite the valiant efforts of two colleagues to save him it took 15 minutes to recover him and he died soon after in hospital But the legacy of Paul's death was that it led directly to the introduction of water safety and rescue equipment on frontline fire appliances nationally and the replacement of traditional hemp lines with floating nylon line

input.evidence_text: The hero firefighter who died trying to save a life More than 25 years after Sub Officer Paul Metcalf died trying to rescue a teenager from Hawkshaw's Simons Lodge, an FBU Red Plaque at Ramsbottom Fire Station honours the hero whose sacrifice transfor News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 16:43, 27 Sep 2026 Updated 17:00, 27 Sep 2026 It was an act of heroism which ended in tragedy. But every firefighter in the UK owes a debt to Paul Metcalf who died trying in vain to save the life of a teenager On a balmy autumn Sunday in 1999 Sub Officer Metcalf, based at Ramsbottom Fire Station and a crew answered a call. A boy had vanished under the surface at Simons Lodge, Hawkshaw. He had slipped into the water from a rope swing hanging from a tree as he tested the temperature with Super fit Mr Metcalf, aged 40, and a karate black belt, dived in but his non-floating rope became snagged on an underwater branch. As colleagues and police pulled the line to bring him ashore, unaware it was caught, he was pulled under water Despite the valiant efforts of two colleagues to save him it took 15 minutes to recover him and he died soon after in hospital But the legacy of Paul's death was that it led directly to the introduction of water safety and rescue equipment on frontline fire appliances nationally and the replacement of traditional hemp lines with floating nylon line

title: Oldham Council agrees interim Lead Member arrangements to strengthen governance and accountability

input.lead: Oldham Council has approved a new package of interim governance arrangements
input.summary: Oldham Council has approved a new package of interim governance arrangements
input.evidence_text: Oldham Council has approved a new package of interim governance arrangements. These measures are designed to strengthen democratic oversight, provide clear political leadership across key service areas and support transparent decision-making while the borough continues to work towards the appointment of a Council Leader and Cabinet. The arrangements were approved by Council on 16 September and include the creation of interim Lead Member and Deputy Lead Member roles aligned to the Council's four directorates. The arrangements form part of a wider governance framework developed following legal advice, engagement with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, and discussions between political group leaders. Under the arrangements, Chief Executive Shelley Kipling will continue to exercise delegated executive powers, while Lead Members provide political oversight, advocacy and a visible link between residents, councillors and services. The roles carry no executive decision-making powers. The four Interim Lead Member portfolios have been allocated to the Council's four largest political groups, with deputy roles assigned from the same groups. Interim Lead Member appointments Resources - Lead Member: Sam Al-Hamdani (Liberal Democrats) - Deputy Lead Member: Mark Kenyon (Liberal Democrats) The Resources portfolio will provide political oversight of the Council's finances, budget management, transformation programme, corporate services, governance, workforce and organisational performance. Place - Lead Member: Arooj Shah (Labour) - Deputy Lead Member: Elaine Taylor (Labour) The Place portfolio will focus on regeneration, economic growth, planning, housing, highways, environmental services, transport and the continued delivery of major projects that support Oldham

title: Council secures court order following unauthorised encampment at Oldham Edge

input.lead: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge
input.summary: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge
input.evidence_text: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge. Council officers first visited the site on Thursday 6th August following concerns from residents and people using the park. Officers spoke to those at the encampment, who said they intended to leave by Saturday 8th August. As the site had not been vacated, the Council returned with support from Greater Manchester Police on Tuesday 11th August. A formal direction was served under Section 77 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, requiring those at the encampment to leave and remove their vehicles and belongings. The Council also provided information about authorised sites in Greater Manchester, along with advice about health, wellbeing and reporting hate crime. After the direction was not followed, the Council began court proceedings. On Monday 17th August, Tameside Magistrates’ Court granted an order requiring the removal of the encampment. The site was vacated later that day. A significant amount of waste was left behind, which has now been removed by the Council’s cleansing team. A Council spokesperson said: “We understand the concerns raised by residents and people using Oldham Edge, and we thank them for their patience while we followed the legal process. “We always try to resolve unauthorised encampments through discussion and voluntary cooperation wherever possible. However, when the site was not vacated as agreed, it became necessary to take further action. “We worked closely with Greater Manchester Police throughout to make sure the situation was handled lawfully and proportionately. “The encampment has now left and our cleansing team has completed the clean-up, allowing the area to be returned to the local community.”

title: Meet the artists bringing Oldham's Town of Culture to life

input.lead: Thirteen local artists, schools, charities and community groups have been chosen to bring their ideas to life during Oldham’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture
input.summary: Thirteen local artists, schools, charities and community groups have been chosen to bring their ideas to life during Oldham’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture
input.evidence_text: Thirteen local artists, schools, charities and community groups have been chosen to bring their ideas to life during Oldham’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture. From theatre, film and music to a new mural and giant fuzzy felt artwork, the projects cover a wide range of art forms and celebrate Oldham’s people, places and stories. Oldham secured the Town of Culture title with its programme, Rising Up. Earlier this year, local creatives were invited to apply for a Town of Culture micro-commission. There were 84 applications, with 13 projects chosen to receive funding. Some of the successful artists and groups recently came together to mark the start of the programme. Not everyone was able to attend, but all 13 projects will play an important part in Oldham’s Town of Culture year. A huge Oldham welcome to: Sew Oldham – Isobel Pickup and Fay Buchanan The Oldham Panorama, a famous view of the town created in 1876, is 150 years old this year. Isobel and Fay will reimagine it for today using patchwork and running-stitch embroidery. Local people will be invited to add buildings and places that are important to them, using old clothes and fabric from home. A New Mural for Oldham – Deggy Art Deggy taught himself how to spray-paint during lockdown, starting with a painting of Joe Exotic. It snowballed from there and his murals can now be seen across Greater Manchester and Derbyshire. He will create a new mural on Oldham’s high street; the subject is a secret for now. input.evidence_text: The Olllam is a band that fuses Irish traditional music with the modern jazz/post-rock energy of Detroit. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round

The next phase of AI is likely to be much less about what a model can demonstrate on a screen and much more about whether businesses can deploy it securel There is also an opportunity for Manchester and the wider North that goes beyond simply increasing AI adoption. The region already has strengths across advanced materials, computing infrastructure, cyber security, health innovation and emerging technologies such as quantum. The c The previous day also saw an Innovation Day, where 20 of the region’s most innovative startups pitched to the biggest organisations working across defence, national security and technology, then took part in a number of Round Table discussions Here’s our write up of the full day’s conference
